posts.title: What we cook in a week
posts.excerpt: Tomás Rivera cooks lunch and the afternoon snack in the house each weekday, and the week's list follows the children who are actually here.
posts.content:
Tomás Rivera starts in the kitchen while the front door is opening. He has cooked at Madoka Childcare since 2016, in the two-storey brick house at 12 Linden Row, Ranelagh, Dublin 6. Lunch is at 11:30. The afternoon snack is at 15:00. Breakfast is there from 07:30 for children who arrive hungry. The kitchen week is Monday to Friday, and then it stops. At weekends, on Irish public holidays, and from 24 December to 1 January, the house is closed and the stove is cold.

Each morning he looks at who is in, what vegetables are on the board, and the notes above the pass. Those notes name allergies, a baby on purées, a toddler moving through baby-led weaning, and a child still learning the spoon. He writes the lunches and snacks for the coming days where families can read them beside the coat hooks. Monday's lunch is cooked on Monday morning. Tuesday's lunch is cooked on Tuesday morning. Wednesday, Thursday and Friday are the same. The dishes change with the season and with the rooms. The shape of the day does not: one cooked lunch, one simple snack, water on the table.

The rooms eat what the kitchen has cooked. Educators sit with the children at the low tables, and the meal is the meal of the house. A Nest baby on purées has purée. A child who is ready for pieces has soft pieces from that same lunch. The pace was agreed at the family meeting, with the key person, before anyone relied on it. Samuel Osei and Priya Raman carry the detail for the Nest, where feeds also happen on demand and a spoon is only part of the story. In the Meadow, Aoife Brennan's children bring strong opinions to the table, which is ordinary at 15 to 30 months. In the Grove, Clara Moreau's children often go from lunch to rest, and later to studio play at 15:30, with paint, water and a wash of hands before anything else is touched.

Food sits inside the fee. There is no second bill from the kitchen. Five days, Monday to Friday, 07:30 to 18:30, is €1,480 a month. Four fixed weekdays are €1,240. Three fixed weekdays are €980. Two days, from 15 months in Meadow and Grove, are €690. Meals, nappies, wipes and sun cream are included. Registration is €150, paid once when you accept a place, and an extra day is €78 if you book it a week ahead and a place is free. None of those amounts is a food surcharge. Families using the National Childcare Scheme still see these euro figures. We provide the statements the scheme asks for, and whatever a family receives depends on that family, not on a number we guess at the door.

Allergies are settled earlier than the morning rush, even though the plate is made every morning. At the family meeting you say what your child must avoid, and what you already do at home. Tomás follows the written note. If a lunch cannot be kept safe, he says so before 07:30 on a day you were counting on him. We will not call this kitchen free of any allergen. The house does not make claims of that kind about food, sleep or later learning. What the kitchen does make is lunch, five days a week, with the children's notes open.

The care day holds the meals in a place you can remember. After garden and outdoor play at 09:30, the house comes in for 11:30. After nap and quiet rest at 12:30, the snack at 15:00 turns the afternoon toward studio play, then stories and first pickups at 17:00, then the last pickup at 18:30. A child in the settling-in fortnight may leave before the snack. That is expected. The fortnight is included in the first month's fee, the days start short, and they grow toward a full day. While the child is here, they eat what the kitchen has for them, and the key person tells you how it went, in plain words, when you come back to the door.

If you want to see the doorway of the kitchen rather than read about it, visit on Tuesday or Thursday at 10:00 or at 16:00. A visit lasts 45 minutes. Hanna Kowalski, family coordinator since 2021, books it, and she will ask your child's age so you are in the right room. Depending on the hour, you will see tables being set or the morning still under way. You can ask what that week's list says. Madoka Quinlan opened the centre in 2015 after twelve years as a room leader. Tomás arrived the following year. The idea, from the start of his time here, is a small house, a known cook, and a day a working parent can picture from the door to 18:30. The phone is +353 1 555 0172. The email is hello@madoka-childcare.example.

posts.title: Why naps don't follow the clock
posts.excerpt: In the Nest, naps and feeds follow each baby; from 12:30 the older rooms rest together.
posts.content:
Babies do not sleep by the clock, so in the Nest we do not ask them to. Each baby has a cot, a blanket from home if you like, and a key person who knows the signs of tiredness.

From 12:30 Meadow and Grove rest together in the quiet room, with curtains half drawn and low cots. Some children sleep, some lie and look at the ceiling, and both are fine.

Tell your key person about a short night. It changes how the morning goes and how early we start the rest.

posts.title: Washing hands, forty times a day
posts.excerpt: A low sink, a stool and an educator at the child's side: how handwashing becomes a habit.
posts.content:
There is a low sink in every room, with a soap dispenser a toddler can press. Hands are washed after the garden, before lunch, after nappies and after painting.

An educator stands beside the child and sings or counts while the water runs. By two and a half, most children in Grove wash their hands on their own and remind the adults.

It is a small habit, repeated all day, and it is one of the things families tell us they see at home.
